title: Presentation of Data
description: Class 11 Economics: tabular presentation and parts of a statistical table, diagrammatic presentation (bar diagrams and pie charts), and graphical presentation (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, time series).

topics.title: Tabular Presentation of Data
topics.concept:
After data are collected and organised, they must be presented in a clear, attractive way so that readers can understand them at a glance. The simplest form is tabular presentation — arranging data in rows and columns in a statistical table.

A good table is far easier to read than a paragraph full of figures. A well-made statistical table has these parts:

  • Table number — for easy reference.
  • Title — states clearly what the table shows (what, where, when).
  • Head note — extra information below the title, e.g. the unit ("in ₹ crore").
  • Captions — the headings of the columns (vertical).
  • Stubs — the headings of the rows (horizontal).
  • Body — the main part containing the actual figures (the data).
  • Footnote — explains anything special about an entry.
  • Source note — states where the data came from (important for trust).

A simple example table:

Table 1: Students by stream, Class 11 (2025)
Stream (stub)BoysGirls
Science4030
Commerce2535

Source: School records (source note)

Here "Boys/Girls" are captions, "Science/Commerce" are stubs, and the numbers form the body.

examples.problem: Example 1: In a statistical table, what are captions and stubs?
examples.solution:
They are the headings.

  • Captions are the column headings (vertical).
  • Stubs are the row headings (horizontal).
examples.answer: Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is a source note important in a table?
examples.solution:
It builds trust.

  • It states where the data came from.
  • This lets readers check the reliability of the figures.
examples.answer: It states where the data came from, so readers can judge the reliability of the figures.

examples.problem: Example 3: Which part of the table contains the actual figures?
examples.solution:
The main area.

  • The body of the table holds the actual data.

recap:
• Tabular presentation = data in rows and columns (a statistical table); clearer than prose.
  • Parts: table number, title, head note, captions (column heads), stubs (row heads), body (the figures), footnote, source note.

quiz.q: The column headings of a statistical table are called:
quiz.explanation: Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings.

quiz.q: The actual figures of a table are contained in its:
quiz.explanation: The body holds the actual data.

topics.title: Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts
topics.concept:
Diagrams turn numbers into pictures that even a non-expert can grasp instantly. Diagrammatic presentation shows data as bars, rectangles or circles. The most common types:

  • Simple bar diagram — a set of equal-width bars whose heights show the values. The taller the bar, the larger the value.
  • Multiple bar diagram — two or more bars are drawn side by side for each category, to compare them (e.g. boys vs girls in each stream).
  • Component (sub-divided) bar diagram — each bar is divided into parts to show the components that make up the total.
  • Pie chart (circle diagram) — a circle divided into slices, where each slice's angle is proportional to its share. Since the whole circle is 360°, the angle of a slice = (component ÷ total) × 360°.

A simple bar diagram of the example data looks like this:

examples.problem: Example 1: In a simple bar diagram, what does the height of a bar represent?
examples.solution:
Bars of equal width vary in height.

  • The height of each bar represents the value of that item.
  • Taller bar = larger value.
examples.answer: The height of a bar represents the value of the item — the taller the bar, the larger the value.

examples.problem: Example 2: A family spends ₹5,000 on food out of a total budget of ₹20,000. What angle would the food slice take in a pie chart?
Example 3: Which diagram is best to compare boys and girls within each stream?
examples.solution:
Two bars per category.

  • A multiple bar diagram draws boys' and girls' bars side by side for each stream.
examples.answer: A multiple bar diagram (side-by-side bars for each category).

recap:
• Bar diagrams: simple (height = value), multiple (compare 2+ bars side by side), component (bar split into parts of a total).
  • Pie chart: circle split into slices; slice angle = (component ÷ total) × 360°.

quiz.q: In a pie chart, the angle of a slice equals:
To compare two or more values for each category side by side, you use a:
quiz.explanation: A multiple bar diagram places several bars side by side per category.

topics.title: Graphical Presentation: Histogram, Polygon and Ogive
topics.concept:
When data are in class intervals (a frequency distribution), we present them as graphs rather than bar diagrams. The main graphs are:

  • Histogram — a set of adjoining rectangles (no gaps between them), where the width of each rectangle is the class interval and the height is the frequency. It looks like a bar chart but the bars touch, because the classes are continuous.
  • Frequency polygon — a line graph formed by joining the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
  • Frequency curve — a smooth, free-hand curve through those mid-points.
  • Ogive (cumulative frequency curve) — a graph of the cumulative frequencies. The "less than" ogive rises from left to right; the "more than" ogive falls. The point where the two ogives cross gives the median.

A separate, important graph is the time series (line) graph — used when data are recorded over time (e.g. yearly GDP). Time is taken on the horizontal axis and the value on the vertical axis, and the points are joined to show the trend (rising, falling or fluctuating) over the period.

examples.problem: Example 1: How does a histogram differ from a simple bar diagram?
examples.solution:
Look at the gaps.

  • In a histogram the rectangles touch (no gaps) because classes are continuous.
  • In a bar diagram the bars are separate.
examples.answer: In a histogram the rectangles are adjoining (no gaps) since the classes are continuous; in a bar diagram the bars are separate.

examples.problem: Example 2: How is a frequency polygon obtained?
examples.solution:
Join the tops of the bars.

  • By joining the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
examples.answer: By joining the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.

examples.problem: Example 3: What does the point where the 'less than' and 'more than' ogives cross give?
examples.solution:
The two cumulative curves meet.

  • Their intersection gives the median of the data.

recap:
• Histogram: adjoining rectangles (no gaps), width = class, height = frequency.
  • Frequency polygon/curve: join the mid-points of the bar tops (straight lines / smooth curve).
  • Ogive = cumulative frequency curve; 'less than' & 'more than' ogives cross at the median.
  • Time series graph: time on x-axis, value on y-axis — shows the trend over time.

quiz.q: A graph with adjoining rectangles (no gaps) for a frequency distribution is a:
quiz.explanation: A histogram has adjoining rectangles because the classes are continuous.

quiz.q: A cumulative frequency curve is called an:
quiz.explanation: The cumulative frequency curve is the ogive.

questions.q: Arranging data in rows and columns is called ____ presentation.
questions.explanation: Rows and columns form tabular presentation.

questions.q: The column headings of a table are called:
questions.explanation: Captions are the column headings.

questions.q: The row headings of a table are called:
questions.explanation: Stubs are the row headings.

questions.q: The part of a table that contains the actual figures is the:
questions.explanation: The body holds the actual data.

questions.q: The note stating where data came from is the:
questions.explanation: The source note states the origin of the data.

questions.q: In a simple bar diagram, the value is shown by the bar's:
questions.explanation: The height of the bar shows the value.

questions.q: Bars drawn side by side to compare categories form a:
questions.explanation: A multiple bar diagram has side-by-side bars.

questions.q: A bar divided into parts to show components of a total is a:
questions.explanation: A component (sub-divided) bar diagram shows parts of a total.

questions.q: In a pie chart, the angle of a slice equals:
questions.explanation: Slice angle = (component ÷ total) × 360°.

questions.q: A component worth one-fourth of the total takes a pie angle of:
A graph of a frequency distribution with adjoining rectangles is a:
questions.explanation: A histogram has adjoining (touching) rectangles.

questions.q: Joining the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars gives a:
questions.explanation: That line graph is the frequency polygon.

questions.q: A cumulative frequency curve is called an:
questions.explanation: The cumulative frequency curve is the ogive.

questions.q: The two ogives (less than and more than) cross at the:
questions.explanation: Their intersection gives the median.

questions.q: Data recorded over time is best shown by a:
questions.explanation: A time series graph shows values over time.

questions.q: A newspaper shows household spending split into food, rent, and savings as slices of a circle. This is a:
questions.explanation: Shares of a whole shown as slices of a circle make a pie chart.

questions.q: If transport is 25% of a family's budget, its pie-chart slice has an angle of:
A histogram's bars touch each other, unlike a bar diagram, because a histogram shows:
options: Continuous class intervals with no gaps
questions.explanation: Continuous classes leave no gaps, so the rectangles adjoin.

questions.q: To show how India's GDP changed each year from 2010 to 2024, the best presentation is a:
questions.explanation: Values over time are best shown as a line (time series) graph revealing the trend.

questions.q: A school wants to show, for each of 3 years, the number of boys and girls separately. The clearest diagram is a:
questions.explanation: Two bars (boys, girls) per year side by side make a multiple bar diagram.

questions.q: An economist wants to read off the median of grouped data graphically. She should draw an:
questions.explanation: The median is read from the ogive (or where the two ogives cross).

questions.q: A table without a source note is weaker mainly because readers:
options: Cannot check where the data came from
questions.explanation: The source note lets readers judge reliability; without it, trust falls.

questions.q: To show the parts that make up a single total within one bar, use a:
questions.explanation: A component bar diagram splits one bar into its parts of the total.

questions.q: Compared with a paragraph of figures, a good table is better because it:
options: Presents data clearly at a glance for easy comparison
questions.explanation: Rows and columns let the eye compare figures quickly — the point of tabulation.

questions.q: Smoothing a frequency polygon into a free-hand curve gives a:
questions.explanation: A smooth curve through the mid-points is the frequency curve.
